## Page Summary

outlined\_flag

- The Programmable Search Element now offers a paid ads-free version for a small fee per search.

- Nonprofit, education, and government users can get an ads-free experience by following specific instructions.

- To use the Paid API, you need a configured Programmable Search Engine and an API key added in the control panel.

- Pricing is $5 per 1000 ad-free search element queries, and billing and quotas should be configured.

- Usage of the Programmable Search Element API can be monitored through the Cloud Platform Console's API Dashboard or the Google Cloud Operations console.


The [Programmable Search\\
Element](https://developers.google.com/custom-search/docs/tutorial/implementingsearchbox) now offers a paid
ads-free version. By enabling the Programmable Search Element Paid API your
Programmable Search Element will continue to function exactly the same as the
free ad-supported version, except that instead of ads being displayed along with
search results you'll instead be charged a small fee for each search.

Note that our nonprofit, education, and government users can get an ads-free
experience by following [these\\
instructions](https://support.google.com/programmable-search/answer/12423873).

## Prerequisites

### Search engine configuration

Before using the Programmable Search Element Paid API you first need to create
and configure your Programmable Search Engine. If you have not already created a Programmable Search Engine, you
can start by visiting the [Programmable Search Engine control panel](https://programmablesearchengine.google.com/controlpanel/all).

Follow the [tutorial](https://developers.google.com/custom-search/docs/tutorial/creatingcse) to learn more
about different configuration options.

### API key

The Programmable Search Element API requires the use of an API key.

If at any point you want to return to the free ad-supported search element, in [Programmable Search Engine control panel](https://programmablesearchengine.google.com/controlpanel/all), navigate to the Ads section of your search engine's
Overview page and delete the key from the "Paid Element API key" field.

## Pricing

The Programmable Search Element API charges $5 per 1000 ad-free search element
queries. [Billing](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/manage-billing-account) needs to be configured in the
API Console. Quotas can be configured in the [Cloud Platform\\
Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/dashboard) to help limit maximum
daily expenditures.

Note that new consumer projects will default to unlimited daily quota; we
_strongly_ recommend setting a [daily quota](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/api/programmablesearchelement.googleapis.com/quotas) that is sufficient for
your traffic volume. Once the daily quota limit is reached all search element
queries using the engine will be denied for the remainder of the day. Note also
that per-minute and per-user per-minute quota controls are also available (with
IP address being used to distinguish between users).

## Monitoring

Two options are available for monitoring usage of the Programmable Search
Element API. First, [Cloud Platform Console's API\\
Dashboard](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/dashboard) provides a variety
of pre-built graphs for monitoring common metrics such as error rates and
queries-per-second. Second, the Google Cloud Operations console provides
powerful tools for building custom graphs and also for setting up alerting. See
[API Monitoring](https://developers.google.com/custom-search/v1/overview#monitoring) for more information.

Google Custom Search JSON API or Google Search API is the official API for retrieving search results in a structured format.

**What this API actually does**

- It lets you send a **search query** (like a keyword or phrase)
- And it returns **structured JSON search results**

(titles, URLs, snippets, etc.)
- You access it using an **API key + Search Engine ID (CX)**

It is **meant for programmatic access**, not UI embedding.

Although it’s programmatic, it **does NOT replicate Google search fully**. And therefore, there are some limitations to using this official API.

Hi, I’m **Darshan Khandelwal**, CTO of [Scrapingdog](https://www.scrapingdog.com/), a web scraping API. Through my experience working with web scraping and extracting Google Search results at scale, I’ve spent significant time understanding how Google search data works and where official APIs fall short.

If you are someone looking to integrate this API into your system or workflows, this is must read for you.

In this article, I’ll walk you through everything you need to know about the Google Custom Search JSON API. We will talk about its features, pricing, usage, and limitations. After that, I’ll introduce a third-party alternative API that we developed at Scrapingdog.

Let’s get started.

## 5 Features of Google Custom Search JSON API

Okay, this is where it gets interesting.

At first, the Google Custom Search JSON API looks like a simple way to access Google search results.

But once you start using it, you realize how the API is structured, what it allows you to do, and where it draws clear boundaries. Understanding these features is important before deciding whether this API fits your use case.

Let’s break down what the Google Custom Search JSON API actually offers.

### 1\. Programmatic search queries

The API allows you to send search queries programmatically using HTTP requests. Each query returns search results in a structured JSON format, making it suitable for applications, scripts, and backend workflows.

### 2\. Structured search result data

Each response includes structured fields such as titles, URLs, snippets, and basic metadata. This makes the data easy to parse, store, and analyze without dealing with raw HTML.

### 3\. Uses a Programmable Search Engine (CX)

To use this API, you must create a Programmable Search Engine and link it using a Search Engine ID (CX).

A **Programmable Search Engine** lets you:

- Define the _scope of your search_ — for example, limit to specific sites or choose to search the wider web.
- Customize **how your search engine behaves and prioritizes results**.
- Get a unique **Search Engine ID (CX)**, which is required to use the Custom Search JSON API.

You can learn more about creating and configuring a Programmable Search Engine in Google’s official docs [here](https://developers.google.com/custom-search/v1/overview).

### 4\. Pagination support

The API supports pagination, allowing you to fetch multiple pages of results for the same query. Each request typically returns up to 10 results, with additional pages accessible through pagination parameters.

### 5\. Official and policy-compliant access

Since this is an official Google API, it operates within Google’s documented policies and usage limits. This makes it suitable for teams that prefer official, documented access to search data.

## **How to Set Up and Access the Google Custom Search JSON API**

Before you can start using the Google Custom Search JSON API, there is a defined setup process that every user must follow. While there is no manual approval is required, the API cannot be used without completing these configuration steps.

### 1\. Create a Google Cloud project

The first step is to create a project in the Google Cloud Console. This project acts as the container where your API usage, quotas, and billing are managed. Every request made to the API is tied to this project.

### 2\. Enable the Custom Search JSON API

Once the Cloud project is created, you must explicitly enable the **Custom Search JSON API** from the API Library. Without enabling the API, requests will not be processed, even if you have an API key.

### 3\. Create a Programmable Search Engine (CX)

To use the API, you must create a **Programmable Search Engine**. This step is mandatory.

The Programmable Search Engine defines what content the API is allowed to search. You can configure it to:

- Search specific websites
- Or search a broader web scope

When the search engine is created, you receive a **Search Engine ID (CX)**, which is required in every API request.

### 4\. Generate an API key

Next, you generate an API key from the Google Cloud Console. This key is used to authenticate requests and track usage. Every API call must include this key along with the CX value.

### 5\. Enable billing for higher usage

The API includes a small free quota, but to exceed it, billing must be enabled on the Cloud project. Billing is automatically applied based on usage and does not require manual approval. Quotas and daily limits are enforced at the project level.

### 6\. Make API requests

After completing these steps, you can start sending search queries programmatically and receive results in JSON format. All usage remains subject to Google’s enforced limits and policies, which cannot be bypassed through configuration.

## 5 Limitations of the Google Custom Search JSON API

The Google Custom Search JSON API provides official and structured access to search results; however, it comes with several built-in limitations that are important to understand before relying on it for production purposes.

Google enforces these limitations through quotas, pricing, and configuration.

As a result, the API works well for small or controlled workloads, but becomes restrictive when deeper results, higher volumes, or broader search coverage are required.

### 1\. Hard daily usage cap

Even with billing enabled, the API enforces a **fixed daily limit of 10,000 queries per project**. This cap cannot be increased through configuration or payment.

Once the daily quota is exhausted, the API stops responding until the next day. This makes it difficult to use the API for applications that require continuous or high-volume search data.

### 2\. Pricing becomes restrictive at scale

The API follows a usage-based pricing model, but costs grow quickly when search volume increases. Since each query is billed individually and daily usage is capped, scaling search operations becomes both **cost-sensitive and volume-restricted**.

For use cases involving hundreds or thousands of keywords per day, pricing and quota limits together become a bottleneck.

### 3\. Dependency on Programmable Search Engine (CX)

Every request must be tied to a **Programmable Search Engine (CX)**. This additional configuration layer defines what the API can search and how results are scoped.

While this works well for controlled environments, it adds friction for workflows that require:

- Dynamic search behavior
- Broad, unrestricted SERP access
- Frequent changes in query scope

### 4\. Limited SERP context

The API provides access to structured search metadata, but it does not expose the **full Google SERP experience**. Many commonly visible search elements are not available, such as:

- _People Also Ask_
- _Local and map-based results_
- _Ads and shopping units_
- _Rich layouts and SERP features_

This limits the API’s usefulness for applications that rely on complete SERP context rather than just organic result links.

### 5\. Not built for large-scale SERP extraction

Because of its fixed daily quota, pricing model, and scoped search behavior, the Google Custom Search JSON API is not designed for:

- _Large-scale SERP monitoring_
- _SEO rank tracking across many keywords_
- _Competitive analysis in depth_
- _Continuous search data pipelines_

The API works best for **low to moderate usage,** where official access is preferred over flexibility or scale.

_What’s next then?_

_If your use case falls into a category where the Google Custom Search JSON API has limitations, the next logical step is to look for alternative options._

## **How Scrapingdog’s Google Search API Addresses These Limitations**

[Scrapingdog’s Google Search API](https://www.scrapingdog.com/google-search-api/) can be used to retrieve structured output data from SERPs.

Unlike the official Google Custom Search JSON API, this API is built for speed and scalability, and it does not enforce a fixed daily request cap in the same way.

You can even test it out on the playground when you [sign up](https://api.scrapingdog.com/register) for the free pack. Unlike the official Google Custom Search JSON API, Scrapingdog does not impose a hard, fixed daily request cap that blocks usage once a threshold is reached.

Instead, usage is governed by credits and plan limits, which allows requests to scale smoothly based on actual demand. This makes it suitable for workloads that require continuous querying or higher daily volumes without abrupt interruptions.

_Scrapingdog’s Google Search API retrieves data directly from live Google search result pages. This allows access to a broader SERP context compared to the official API, which only returns limited metadata. As a result, users can work with richer and more complete search result data for analysis, monitoring, and automation._

## Conclusion

Choosing the right Google search API ultimately depends on your use case and budget.

The official Google Custom Search JSON API works well for low to moderate usage where official access, clear documentation, and strict compliance are priorities.

However, as search data needs grow, be it in terms of volume, frequency, or SERP completeness, the limitations around daily caps, pricing, and flexibility become more noticeable.

In such cases, a third-party solution like Scrapingdog’s Google Search API can be a practical alternative, offering greater scalability and fewer operational constraints.

Before making a decision, it’s important to evaluate how much search data you need, how often you need it, and how critical flexibility and scale are for your workflow. Aligning these factors with the right API will help you build a more reliable and cost-effective solution.

Hi Mark,

There is no cost when using Programmable Search Engine as such. Please review the current offerings:

[https://support.google.com/programmable-search/answer/9069107?hl=en](https://support.google.com/programmable-search/answer/9069107?hl=en)

There are different ways one can implement Programmable Search Engine and one of the way is using Custom Search JSON API.

Custom Search JSON API provides 100 search queries per day for free. If you need more, you may sign up for billing in the API Console. Additional requests cost $5 per 1000 queries, up to 10k queries per day:

https://developers.google.com/custom-search/v1/overview

The first 100 queries per day are free, and they do not "roll over". Billing does not happen on a per-day basis and it's not done in 1000 query "lots". The $5 per 1000 is just the rate.

Suppose you make 200 queries today, and 110 queries tomorrow (and nothing else), you will be billed for 110 (100+10) queries i.e 5/1000 \* 110, or $0.55.

## Page Summary

outlined\_flag

- The Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API will cease to serve traffic on January 8, 2025, requiring customers to transition to Google Cloud's Vertex AI Search.

- This API is for Programmable Search Engines restricted to searching 10 or fewer specific sites with no daily query limit.

- Using this API with a configuration that doesn't meet the site restriction rules may result in unexpected results.

- Requests to the Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API cost $5 per 1000 queries with no daily limit.


This document describes how to use the Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API.

## About the Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API

If your Programmable Search Engine is restricted to only searching specific sites (10 or fewer),
you can use the Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API. This API is similar to the
Custom Search JSON API except this version has no daily query limit. To use this
version, confirm that you see 10 or fewer sites to search in the “Sites to
Search” section of your Programmable Search Engine control panel, there are no global top level
domain patterns, and that “Search the entire web” is set to OFF.

When using the Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API endpoint, be mindful that if your
Programmable Search Engine configuration is changed so that it does not conform with the site
restriction rules above, the Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API may not return the
expected results.

## Making a request

Making a request to Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API is similar to making a request to
Custom Search JSON API; however, the URI is different. The format for the
Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API is

https://www.googleapis.com/customsearch/v1/siterestrict?\[parameters\]

The `[parameters]` are the same as the [Custom Search JSON API](https://developers.google.com/custom-search/v1/using_rest) parameters

## Pricing

Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API requests cost $5 per 1000 queries and there is no
daily query limit. You may sign up for [billing](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/manage-billing-account) in the
API Console.

> ![:warning:](https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/warning.png?v=15)**Deprecation Notice (March 2026):** Google has discontinued the “Search the entire web” option for Programmable Search Engines. New search engines now require at least one specific site to be configured. Additionally, the Custom Search JSON API is being replaced by Vertex AI Search. The Discourse AI team is actively researching alternative web search providers and plans to ship new search tools soon — including support for native LLM provider search (e.g. Gemini’s built-in search). This guide remains useful for existing setups, but be aware of these limitations when creating new configurations.

## [Heading link](https://meta.discourse.org/t/google-search-for-discourse-ai-programmable-search-engine-and-custom-search-api/307107\#p-1512433-google-search-for-discourse-ai-1) Google Search for Discourse AI

To set up a Google search bot with the Discourse AI plugin, you will need to configure a Google Programmable Search Engine and Custom Search API key. Whichever AI model you use will need to use this search tool to return Google search results. When you set up an AI service for your Discourse Plugin, for example if you are using OpenAI API GPT or Anthropic Claude, and you want to use a helper bot to do Google searches, you will need to configure a Programmable Search Engine to search Google with and an API key for your researcher bot to access the search engine and return results.

### [Heading link](https://meta.discourse.org/t/google-search-for-discourse-ai-programmable-search-engine-and-custom-search-api/307107\#p-1512433-introduction-google-cloud-programmable-search-engine-and-custom-search-api-2) Introduction: Google Cloud, Programmable Search Engine and Custom Search API

The [Programmable Search Engine](https://developers.google.com/custom-search/docs/overview) (or Custom Search Engine) is a free search engine service that anyone can set up on their website and is identified by a search engine ID (or CX number). A Custom Search API key is used to make API requests to the search engine, and API keys are managed from the [Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com/). Thus, you will need to set up a Google Cloud account - a credit card is required to register your account, but the Custom Search API provides 100 search queries per day for free before you pay (additional requests cost $5 per 1,000 queries, up to 10,000 queries per day, but you will have to buy more usage). See [how to manage billing](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/manage-billing-account).

You will also want to set up your key under a Google Cloud project, preferably a new one designated for the search key (for easier tracking). Note that Google Cloud has quotas on both the number of projects and the number of projects attached to a billing account, and projects can be added to billing accounts after they are set up and API keys are created.

**Checklist**

- Set up Google Cloud account
- Create a project for your custom search API key
- Connect project to billing account
- Create API key
- Configure API key for Custom Search
- Set up a Google Programmable Search Engine
- Save custom search API key and custom search ID in Discourse AI settings

* * *

### [Heading link](https://meta.discourse.org/t/google-search-for-discourse-ai-programmable-search-engine-and-custom-search-api/307107\#p-1512433-step-1-set-up-a-project-in-google-cloud-3) Step 1: Set up a Project in Google Cloud

Before you set up your custom search engine and API key, set up a project in Google Cloud.

Go to [Google Cloud admin for APIs](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials) for you (or your organization), and make sure you are in the parent organization (you can see it in the field at the top next to the Google Cloud logo).

You will have to create a project for your search engine if you haven’t got one already that you want to use - the link to select or create a new project is near the top of the page.

[![Screenshot 2024-05-07 at 9.04.04 AM](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/optimized/4X/a/0/5/a052540cad7024ab9e108f191bf9a5e42ed54b96_2_690x319.jpeg)\\
Screenshot 2024-05-07 at 9.04.04 AM2320×1074 211 KB](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/original/4X/a/0/5/a052540cad7024ab9e108f191bf9a5e42ed54b96.jpeg "Screenshot 2024-05-07 at 9.04.04 AM")

Complete the create new project page (make sure your organization is selected in the appropriate dropdown fields).

[![image](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/original/4X/6/e/2/6e2a062a67a07a1c69aad5c7d78539ac2ad8e42f.png)\\

For managing billing for your project, you will need to set up a billing account for the project in [Google Cloud billing](https://console.cloud.google.com/billing/projects), assuming you have billing configured for your organization. You (or your billing account manager) should be able to do this later after the key is created. Note that there are quotas on projects and billing projects depending on your organization’s Google Cloud account.

To enable billing on your project, go to the Billing tab in the Google Cloud navigation menu and link a billing account, or enable billing for the project from the [billing projects page](https://console.cloud.google.com/billing/projects).

### [Heading link](https://meta.discourse.org/t/google-search-for-discourse-ai-programmable-search-engine-and-custom-search-api/307107\#p-1512433-step-2-create-an-api-key-4) Step 2: Create an API Key

To create an API key from Google Cloud Console, go to the API & Services tab in your Google Cloud console and the [Credential settings](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials) for your new project. (Don’t worry about the “configure consent screen” message). Click the “+ create credentials” link near the top of the page and select “API key” from the drop-down options.

[![image](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/optimized/4X/5/f/5/5f52ee5a4192ab668504c09a4363b5bfddb46d53_2_690x246.png)\\

A new API key will be created for you. Copy and secure it in a safe place like a password vault application. Do not share keys.

[![IMG_1569](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/optimized/4X/2/c/5/2c516da6b5fd023d0d2d3245b8275b8db613705d_2_414x244.jpeg)\\

This is the Google Custom Search API key you will need to enter in your Discourse AI settings for `ai_google_custom_search_api_key`

[![image](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/optimized/4X/8/9/9/899f4310b35e218bc39c6e9411a7a81f48f51321_2_517x123.png)\\

You should now see your new key listed in the API keys list. Click the 3 dots in the Actions column on the far right and select “Edit API key”.

[![image](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/optimized/4X/0/f/0/0f04ed6504f68b473913bfa62d4c6a30cc2f8c36_2_690x150.png)\\

This will bring up the API key credentials configuration page, and here you can edit the name of the API key to something more appropriate. (You can also view/copy your API key or regenerate it if necessary). Then go to the “API restrictions” section at the bottom and select “Restrict key” then choose “Custom Search API”. Click OK and then Save your API key.

To create a search engine for your API key to use, go to the [Google Programmable Search Engine](https://programmablesearchengine.google.com/) page and click “Get started” if you aren’t already logged in (log in or create your account). Once logged in, go to the [search engine console page](https://programmablesearchengine.google.com/controlpanel/all). All your existing programmable search engines will be listed here.

Click the “Add” button (or the “Create your first search engine!” link) to open the new search engine page. Give it a suitable name and fill out the fields as applicable.

> ![:warning:](https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/warning.png?v=15)**Note:** Google now requires at least one site to be configured when creating a Programmable Search Engine, and the “Search the entire web” toggle has been removed. You will need to add at least one site (e.g. `*.example.com/*`) to proceed. This limits results to the configured sites rather than searching the entire web.

[![Screenshot 2024-05-07 at 9.15.50 AM](https://d11a6trkgmumsb.cloudfront.net/optimized/4X/3/9/e/39e4856cb4c0820b120a92bf5dd1506a62507877_2_389x500.png)\\

The page will give you an option to copy the search script if you want to use the search box in a web interface somewhere, but that isn’t necessary here, since we are only interested in using it for our API key credentials to access.

Select the customize button to go to the search engine overview page. Here we can now see the Search Engine ID (CX number) needed for our Discourse AI Google search settings, as well as some other options it’s possible to configure.
